The primary goal of the BS in Interdisciplinary Applied Artificial Intelligence is to prepare graduates who can apply artificial intelligence responsibly, creatively, and effectively across domains, integrating technical skills with ethical reasoning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and real-world problem solving.
The program emphasizes applied and lifelong learning, workforce relevance, and societal impact, ensuring that graduates are prepared for both immediate employment and long- term career adaptability.
It advances student success, retention, timely degree completion, and career readiness.
The program’s applied focus, interdisciplinary design, and integration of experiential learning opportunities support students in developing market- relevant skills that align with workforce needs.
By embedding internships, project-based learning, and applied AI coursework throughout the curriculum, the program enhances students’ engagement, persistence, and post-graduation outcomes while positioning URI graduates to succeed in a rapidly evolving, AI-enabled economy.

The vision is to provide students with deep knowledge of AI systems and expertise in transferring and applying AI to a variety of problem types.
This program will cover knowledge of the AI ecosystem including the ability to work in interdisciplinary teams with data and domain experts to collect, clean organize, and sample data, match the problem and data to the right intelligent computational tool (there are many types of AI, each with its strengths and weaknesses), tailor, build on top of, and adapt these tools to the problems at hand, support the safe, secure, ethical and accurate reporting of the results to domain experts, and guide teams in deciding if the analytical results make sense.
Students will learn how to use, tailor and augment AI so that the AI can serve as assistants in problem solving, with the human as the master, well versed in the interpretation, and ethical and societal implications of the use of the powerful AI that they will wield.
All of this is in the context of a world in which educators and potential employers are concerned with the lack of digital skills among today’s students and graduates.

To be well educated and prepared for the modern workplace, students must learn to acquire applied technology skills and also to transfer these technologies to specific problems as they arise.
Thus this program is not intended to train students to develop new AI, but to become experts in mastering, adapting, building upon, and deploying existing and evolving intelligent computational artifacts.
We will help students to master the AI tools of today but also help them to understand that these are only contemporary examples to sharpen their problem solving, and learning skills, and give them a leg up as they enter the workplace.
As the world changes and embraces new technologies such as digital twins, and quantum computing, both already inextricably intertwined with AI, we propose a major that is flexible enough that it can evolve with emerging intelligent technologies.
The program advances the University’s goals by preparing students to address complex real-world challenges through the responsible and creative application of emerging technologies.

The curriculum integrates applied coursework, project-based learning, and internships, ensuring that students develop both technical expertise and transferable skills that support career readiness and lifelong learning.
The program reflects the University’s commitment to interdisciplinary problem-solving and collaboration across colleges and departments.
The program also contributes to the University’s role in supporting economic development, innovation, and the future of work in Rhode Island and beyond.

Proposed The Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies (BIS) program provides a foundational framework for intellectual development among a diverse community of students.
The courses are designed to challenge students to discover the synergies that exist between and within discipline areas while fostering meaningful interaction with other students who bring expertise from their own areas.
The result is truly interdisciplinary by encouraging deeper learning, both in the student’s own areas and by exposing diverse connections with their classmates.
The BIS program speaks directly to the Strategy 1 Agenda for Change in that students will have the opportunity to explore a range of courses designed to challenge and reflect upon disparities amongst groups.
As a result, students will be encouraged to broaden their thinking as it applies to academia and the world.
Available courses will be from across disciplines such as leadership, economics, nursing, human development/health studies, communication studies, theater, and film.

This major equips students with the knowledge, skills, and hands-on classroom experience needed to succeed as a K-6 teacher and to be eligible for licensure as an elementary teacher in Rhode Island. Existing Elementary Education (grades 1-6).
This major provides the knowledge, skills, and experiences required to be a successful grades 1-6 teacher and prepares teacher candidates to be eligible for licensure as an elementary teacher.
The professional sequence courses taken prior to junior year include: EDC102, EDC250, EDC312, EDC330; prior to Practical Teaching Residency II: EDC402, EDC423, EDC424, EDC452, EDC453, EDC454, EDC455, EDC456, EDC457, EDC458, EDC459.
To be eligible for the practical teaching residency I and II (EDC460, EDC462; EDC484, EDC485) students must maintain a grade point average of 2.50 overall; 2.50 in the major; and a C or above in the EDC professional sequence courses.

We are changing the program description to more accurately reflect the new grade band (K-6) instituted by the Rhode Island Department of Education, eliminating the C or better requirement for EDC 102 & EDC 312 for consistency in expectations across the college, and streamlining the general academic and admission requirements for consistency across the college.
Existing The program has moved to a full-year residency model and is responding to increased curriculum content requirements.
EDC 460, retitled to Practical Teaching Residency I, will move from 2 to 4 credits to account for the additional time in the classroom in the first semester of their residency year.
A seminar to support the first residency semester, EDC 462, was designed and piloted in F24 and we are bringing that course forward for approval at this time.
A total of 5 credits will be added to the major due to this change.
We are adding EDC 330 (3) Intro to M ultilingual Learners as we are following the conversations at the state and national level regarding the preparation of teachers to teach multilingual learns.

EDC 330 will serve the function of introducing students to the needs of multilingual learners in regular education environments.
We anticipate we will need an additional class in the future but we will wait to see what the state will require before doing this.
Some of our students already take this course and have been overwhelming positive in relating how useful it has been to them while in their first year of the program where they are very likely to have students who speak languages other than English in their classroom.
An additional 3 credits will be added to the program.
EDC 452, 455, 456, 457, 458, our elementary methods classes will each add an additional credit due increased content are curriculum requirements, grade level specific student content standards, and the impact of HQIM on the content teachers teach.
The Evaluation course, then, must also address HQIM requirements, in designing or using assessments.
A total of 5 credits will be added to the major.
